Prison
PRIZ-n
n. (rendering Hebrew beth ha-sōhar/masgēr, Greek phylakē/desmōtērion)
From French prison, Latin prensio, a seizing, from prehendo, to take hold of — the place of those who have been taken. Greek phylakē is literally a guarding or watch, the same word used for the watches of the night, so that a prison is named for the guard rather than for the walls.

Biblical Definition

Scripture is full of prisons, and remarkably free of the assumption that they are proof of guilt. Joseph, Jeremiah, Micaiah, John the Baptist, Peter, and Paul were all in them, and God's people are commanded to remember such: “I was in prison, and ye came unto me” (Matthew 25:36), where the Lord identifies Himself so closely with His imprisoned people that visiting them is visiting Him. The messianic commission promises release: the Servant is sent “to open the blind eyes, to bring out the prisoners from the prison, and them that sit in darkness out of the prison house” (Isaiah 42:7), a liberty first spiritual and finally complete. At Philippi God shows what a prison is worth against Him: “suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken” (Acts 16:26) — and the astonishing detail is that the prisoners did not run, so that the gaoler was converted before dawn. And Peter records a preaching in a place no man could visit: Christ “went and preached unto the spirits in prison” (1 Peter 3:19). Whatever the difficulty of that verse, its plain force is that no confinement is beyond His reach or His voice. The doctrine of prison in Scripture is therefore twofold: the state may lawfully hold men, and it repeatedly holds the wrong ones; and God is not shut out of any cell.

Webster 1828 Definition

A place of confinement for those seized or condemned; a gaol. In Scripture, the prison in which the righteous are so often found, Christ counting a visit to the imprisoned as done to Himself, the Servant sent to bring prisoners out of the prison house, and the prison at Philippi shaken to its foundations.

PRISON, n. 1. A house or place of confinement, particularly for debtors and criminals; a gaol.

2. Any place of confinement or involuntary restraint.

3. Figuratively, a state of bondage from which one cannot free himself.

4. From French prison, Latin prehensio, a seizing, from prehendo, to seize.

5. In Scripture, I was in prison, and ye came unto me, Matt. 25; the foundations of the prison were shaken, Acts 16.

Key Scripture

Matthew 25:36 — "Naked, and ye clothed me: I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me."

Isaiah 42:7 — "To open the blind eyes, to bring out the prisoners from the prison, and them that sit in darkness out of the prison house."

Acts 16:26 — "And suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken: and immediately all the doors were opened, and every one's bands were loosed."

1 Peter 3:19 — "By which also he went and preached unto the spirits in prison;"

Modern Corruption

Imprisonment is read as a reliable index of guilt, so that the church forgets a duty Christ commanded; while in the other direction, the state's lawful power of the sword is denied altogether and justice reduced to therapy.

expand to see more

Matthew 25:36 places visiting the imprisoned among the acts by which Christ identifies His own, and the church has often found it the easiest of them to neglect. Part of the reason is a quiet assumption that a man in prison has earned his place there, and therefore that ministry to him is optional charity rather than commanded duty. Scripture's own roll of prisoners — Joseph on a false accusation, Jeremiah in the dungeon of Malchiah, John the Baptist for naming a king's adultery, Paul in chains for the hope of Israel — forbids the assumption. The Lord does not distinguish, in that passage, between the justly and unjustly held; He commands the visit. And the gospel has always found prisons unusually fruitful ground, because a man there has fewer illusions left about his own condition.

The opposite error denies the magistrate's sword. Romans 13 gives the civil ruler a real ministry of justice, bearing the sword to execute wrath upon evildoers, and Scripture nowhere treats punishment as a failure of compassion. Where the state is stripped of that office and crime is reclassified wholly as illness, the wronged are left without redress and the wrongdoer without the moral seriousness of being held responsible — which is itself a denial of his dignity as a man made in God's image and answerable for his acts. The principle to recover holds both: justice is God's ordinance and must be done, and mercy to the imprisoned is God's command and must be shown. Paul sang at midnight in a gaol he had done nothing to deserve, and the gaoler who had locked him in was washing his stripes before morning.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew beth ha-sōhar, the round house or prison of Joseph; masgēr, a lock-up or dungeon; Greek phylakē, a guard or ward, and desmōtērion, a place of bonds.

expand to see more

Hebrew sōhar (H5470) — a round tower or prison; “the prison, a place where the king's prisoners were bound” (Genesis 39:20).

Hebrew masgēr (H4525) — a lock-up or dungeon; “them that sit in darkness out of the prison house” (Isaiah 42:7).

Hebrew bōr (H953) — a pit or cistern used as a dungeon; Jeremiah was let down into one with cords (Jeremiah 38:6).

Greek phylakē (G5438) — a guarding, a watch, and hence a prison; the word of Matthew 25:36 and 1 Peter 3:19.

Greek desmōtērion (G1201) — a place of bonds; the prison at Philippi whose foundations were shaken (Acts 16:26).

Usage

"Of Christ identified with His imprisoned people: I was in prison, and ye came unto me (Matthew 25:36)."

"Of the Servant's commission: to bring out the prisoners from the prison (Isaiah 42:7)."

"Of God's power over any confinement: the foundations of the prison were shaken (Acts 16:26)."
